evidence.claim: A forest reservoir and a charcoal kiln mark the journey to Walker.
evidence.quote: Lynx Lake, Arizona, is a 55-acre (220,000 m2) reservoir located within Prescott National Forest

evidence.claim: A forest reservoir and a charcoal kiln mark the journey to Walker.
evidence.quote: The Walker Charcoal Kiln is a structure in the Prescott National Forest near the town of Walker, Arizona

evidence.claim: The Walker Road corridor takes in Lynx Lake in the Bradshaw Mountains and the settlement of Walker.
evidence.quote: The lake was formed in 1963 when Arizona Game and Fish completed a dam in Lynx Creek, 6 miles (9.7 km) below Walker, Arizona.

evidence.claim: At the lake, ponderosa pine grows alongside beargrass, cliff-rose and alligator juniper.
evidence.quote: Plant life in the area consists of ponderosa pine, beargrass, cliff-rose, and alligator juniper.

evidence.claim: Yavapai County adopted Walker Road as a Scenic/Historic Route on June 21, 2023.
evidence.quote: Walker Road was adopted as a Scenic/Historic Route on June 21, 2023.

evidence.claim: The nearby Walker Charcoal Kiln preserves an older industrial connection: its interpretive sign credits Jake and Joe Carmichael with building it around 1880 to turn oak into fuel for smelters.
evidence.quote: A sign posted near the kiln reads, "This kiln was constructed around 1880 by Jake and Joe Carmichael to convert oak wood into charcoal for use at nearby smelters.

evidence.claim: Traveling toward Walker, Lynx Lake comes first, six miles below the settlement.
evidence.quote: 6 miles (9.7 km) below Walker, Arizona.

evidence.claim: The kiln lies near Walker in Prescott National Forest, in the vicinity of the abandoned Poland Junction Mine near Renegade Hill’s summit.
evidence.quote: situated in the vicinity of the abandoned Poland Junction Mine near the summit of Renegade Hill.

evidence.claim: The journey ends at the community named for nineteenth-century mountain man Joseph R. Walker.
evidence.quote: The settlement was named after 19th-century mountain man Joseph R. Walker.

evidence.claim: Lynx Lake began with a dam: Arizona Game and Fish completed the barrier across Lynx Creek in 1963, six miles below Walker.
evidence.quote: The lake was formed in 1963 when Arizona Game and Fish completed a dam in Lynx Creek, 6 miles (9.7 km) below Walker, Arizona.

evidence.claim: The reservoir sits at 5,530 feet in Prescott National Forest, in the Bradshaw Mountains.
evidence.quote: The lake is located at 5,530 feet (1,690 m) elevation

evidence.claim: Ponderosa pine, alligator juniper, beargrass and cliff-rose grow in the area.
evidence.quote: Plant life in the area consists of ponderosa pine, beargrass, cliff-rose, and alligator juniper.

evidence.claim: A later mechanical problem changed the lake’s story: in December 2024, Arizona Game and Fish announced plans to drain it because an outlet valve had failed in the open position.
evidence.quote: In December 2024 the Arizona Game and Fish Department announced that the lake would be drained due to a mechanical failure that caused an outlet valve to remain in the open position.

evidence.claim: The Walker Charcoal Kiln links the forest to the smelters that used charcoal made from its oak.
evidence.quote: to convert oak wood into charcoal for use at nearby smelters.

evidence.claim: A sign at the kiln credits Jake and Joe Carmichael with its construction around 1880.
evidence.quote: This kiln was constructed around 1880 by Jake and Joe Carmichael

evidence.claim: The same sign explains that charcoal production and mine props required heavy cutting of the surrounding forest in the late nineteenth century.
evidence.quote: The surrounding forest was cut so heavily for charcoal and mine props in the late 1800s

evidence.claim: The structure stands near Renegade Hill’s summit, in the vicinity of the abandoned Poland Junction Mine.
evidence.quote: situated in the vicinity of the abandoned Poland Junction Mine near the summit of Renegade Hill.

evidence.claim: Walker carries the name of nineteenth-century mountain man Joseph R. Walker.
evidence.quote: The settlement was named after 19th-century mountain man Joseph R. Walker.

evidence.claim: Its population fell from 200 in 1890 to 39 in 1920.
evidence.quote: Walker's population was 200 in 1890, and 39 in 1920.

evidence.claim: The settlement stands at an estimated elevation of 6,289 feet above sea level.
evidence.quote: It has an estimated elevation of 6,289 feet (1,917 m) above sea level.

evidence.claim: in Prescott National Forest, in the Bradshaw Mountains.
evidence.quote: reservoir located within Prescott National Forest, approximately 5 miles (8.0 km) east of Prescott, Arizona, in the Bradshaw Mountains.

evidence.claim: in Prescott National Forest
evidence.quote: The Walker Charcoal Kiln is a structure in the Prescott National Forest near the town of Walker, Arizona

evidence.claim: Native animals in the area include mule deer, bald eagles, osprey and javelinas.
evidence.quote: Animals native to the area include mule deer, bald eagles, osprey, and javelinas.

flags: Sparse cache: the county page establishes only the June 21, 2023 county designation, not its rationale, detailed road character, length, construction or campaign history. Overview and moments remain short; no state designation asserted.

Dropped current claims unsupported by cache: Highway 69 departure, road following Lynx Creek, continuous pine cover, forest/private-land halves, mining-claim subdivisions, 100-mailbox pavement endpoint, unpaved continuation toward Mount Union, 1967 paving, 1863 panning party, lynx naming story, placer-gold superlative, mining decline, 1909 fire and 1940 post-office closure.

Smelter Hill omitted because no cache page documents Howell’s 1882 smelter town or that hill. The linked designation application is not saved. Replaced with the documented Walker Charcoal Kiln, marked separate excursion because access is not established.

Lynx Lake cache reports a December 2024 valve failure and announced draining, with no subsequent status. No present water-level, boating, trail-access or closure claim is made. No driving restriction is documented, so no practical note added.
Walker settlement cache does not establish a mining-town history, but the nearby kiln supports retaining the existing mining-town motif for the corridor.
